content.title: Seven shootings in five days: Brussels drug war escalates
content.lead: The Belgian Interior Minister spoke of a «national emergency.» Authorities announced new measures in the fight against drug trafficking. But the problem has long since spiraled out of control.

content.caption: Bullet hole in the sidewalk: Shootings linked to the drug scene repeatedly occur in the Brussels district of Anderlecht.
content.author: Olivier Matthys / EPA

content.text: It began on a Friday evening: Shortly before midnight, two men appeared in front of a police station in the Brussels district of Anderlecht. One filmed with his mobile phone while the other fired twelve shots at the entrance door with a Kalashnikov assault rifle. The two then fled on an electric scooter. Because the station was closed at the time of the attack, no one was injured. Authorities suspected a retaliatory act by a criminal gang – the police had carried out several raids in the drug scene during the summer.

The violence did not abate in the following days. On Saturday evening, a man was injured in the leg by a gunshot in the Saint-Gilles district. Early on Sunday morning, a bullet pierced the window of a bedroom where the resident was still in bed. On Monday, a man opened fire near the Bruxelles-Midi train station with an automatic weapon, forcing the guests of a pizzeria to take cover.
By Tuesday, Brussels authorities had recorded a total of seven shootings within five days. Authorities linked all incidents to drug crime. What is happening in Brussels?

For years, the Belgian capital has been fighting criminal gangs involved in the drug trade, some of whom are rivals. The situation is particularly precarious in the structurally weak west of the city with a high proportion of migrants, for example in Anderlecht. However, in recent years, drug crime has increasingly spread to the wealthier east. As dealers get younger, cocaine gets cheaper, and violence becomes more brutal, authorities are progressively losing control.

content.text: In 2025, there was a record number of 101 shootings, in which a total of 8 people were killed and 43 injured. This year, the figures are similarly high: So far, 66 shootings with 25 injured and 2 dead have been recorded.

Drug crime in the capital has long occupied national politics. Belgian Interior Minister Bernard Quintin said on Thursday morning: «The fight against organized crime associated with drug trafficking is a national emergency.» He announced that the police presence in the affected neighborhoods would be increased, adding that the areas needed to be «flooded» with police officers.

Representatives of national and municipal authorities had already met for a crisis meeting on Wednesday evening. Among other things, authorities decided to send forty additional police officers to the affected municipalities and districts and to install twenty mobile cameras in the coming days. They also decided that a coordination office would be established to improve the information flow between the police, municipalities, and regional authorities.

Whether these measures will have the desired effect is questionable, however. Even before the latest escalation, the Interior Ministry had sent 77 additional police officers to Brussels and provided funds for surveillance cameras. In addition, police have been patrolling metro stations and train stations with soldiers since spring. However, the current legal situation does not allow military personnel to carry out arrests or searches on their own initiative. So far, none of the measures taken have led to a significant reduction in drug crime.

Therefore, authorities are now openly considering much sharper steps: Mayors of the Brussels municipalities were informed at Wednesday's crisis meeting that they could impose curfews or establish zones to which only residents have access.

Such measures, however, would restrict the population, who are already suffering the most from the situation. Many are losing patience: Several organizations have called for a demonstration on Sunday at a well-known drug dealing hotspot in Saint-Gilles. But the dealers will not be driven away by that either.

playableVideoTeasers.title: NZZ Format | Europe's new cocaine front – how drug gangs are infiltrating Spain's coastal towns
playableVideoTeasers.description: For years, cocaine use has been rising in Europe, generating lucrative business for criminal gangs. Now, southern Spain is becoming an increasingly important hub for smugglers. For the people in the tranquil coastal towns, this has sometimes had dramatic consequences. Many tourists appreciate Andalusia for its stunning beaches, idyllic villages, and cozy tapas bars. But Europe's southernmost region also has another face: Here, criminal gangs are expanding, supplying all of Europe with cocaine. «We have a veritable drug economy here,» says social worker Alma Jugado. Andalusia is one of the poorest regions in Spain. Drug smugglers here earn more in a single night than others do in a month. So-called TikTok narcos—influencers who portray the smuggler's life as a big party—contribute to the popularity of the illegal trade. Law enforcement is forced to conduct increasingly dangerous operations while simultaneously becoming increasingly powerless. The documentary delves deep into Andalusia's smuggling business. She accompanies customs officers, social workers – and an investigative journalist who wants to meet with one of the masterminds behind the drug gangs. It becomes clear that the rising crime in southern Spain is far more than a local problem.

playableVideoTeasers.title: NZZ Format | Europe's new drug crisis? How fentanyl and other synthetic opioids threaten us
playableVideoTeasers.description: Highly potent synthetic opioids have killed thousands of people in North America. Now they are appearing in Europe, putting local drug policies to the test. When fentanyl emerged in Vancouver, there was hardly any warning. Within a few years, it largely displaced heroin from the illegal drug market, and the number of fatal overdoses rose dramatically. «I pray that Europe doesn't end up in the same situation as us,» says Canadian addiction specialist Paxton Bach. «But I fear it's only a matter of time.» Meanwhile, highly potent synthetic opioids like Nitazene are also spreading in Europe. They are sold online, mixed with heroin or pills, and sometimes consumed without the users' knowledge. Even the smallest excess can trigger a fatal overdose. In Germany, the fundamental changes in the drug market are becoming apparent. Clinics are increasingly treating younger users; at the same time, the trade is shifting from the streets to the internet. The substances can be ordered with just a few clicks via social networks, messaging apps, and online shops. This makes it harder to reach users with traditional support services and to identify new developments in the market. Since the dismantling of the open drug scenes at Zurich's Platzspitz and Letten districts, Switzerland has been considered a global model of pragmatic drug policy. Supervised consumption sites, substitution programs, drug checking, and early warning systems are intended to prevent isolated incidents from escalating into new crises. But can this successful model of the 1990s withstand a globalized, synthetic drug market?
